blocks.content: Himachal Pradesh has a very rich and ancient history dating back to prehistoric times. The region was inhabited by various tribes and peoples long before recorded history. Archaeological evidence found in the Sirmaur and Kangra districts suggests human habitation as far back as the Stone Age. The Kols (Mundas or Dravidians) were the earliest known inhabitants before the Indo-Aryan migration.

During the Vedic period, the region was described in the Mahabharata and Ramayana. The Trigarta kingdom (present-day Kangra) is mentioned in the Mahabharata; King Susharma of Trigarta sided with the Kauravas. The Rig Veda references the Beas (Vipasa) and the Sutlej (Shutudri) rivers. The Pandavas are believed to have passed through these hills during their exile.

blocks.content: The Mauryan Empire extended into the hill regions. Ashoka's rock edicts mention 'Himalaya-vasi' (hill people). The Gupta period (4th–6th century CE) saw cultural development and active trade routes. After the decline of the Gupta Empire, several small independent hill kingdoms emerged that maintained their independence for centuries.

After the fall of the Gupta Empire, the region saw the rise of many small Rajput hill kingdoms. These kingdoms maintained independence for long periods and resisted various invasions including the Mughals and later the Gurkhas.

blocks.content: The Katoch dynasty is claimed to be one of the oldest royal dynasties in the world, with a lineage of over 3,500 years tracing back to the ancient Trigarta kingdom. The Kangra Fort, one of the oldest and largest forts in the Himalayas, was their stronghold. The fort is built on a hillock at the junction of rivers Manjhi and Banganga.

items: Susharma Chandra: Fought in the Mahabharata war on the side of Kauravas against Pandavas.
Mahmud of Ghazni attacked Kangra (Nagarkot) in 1009 CE and looted its famous temple.
Kangra Fort was captured by Mughal general Shaikh Farid in 1620 CE under Emperor Jahangir.
Sansar Chand (1775–1823 CE): The greatest Kangra ruler; great patron of the Kangra School of Painting. Defeated by Gurkhas in 1806 at Mahal Morian; sought Ranjit Singh's help afterward.
Anirudh Chand: Last Kangra ruler. Kangra became part of British India after Treaty of Lahore (1846).
Kangra School of Painting flourished under Sansar Chand; characterized by lyrical naturalism, Krishna–Radha themes, and soft colors.

blocks.content: The Chamba kingdom was founded around 920 CE by Raja Sahil Varman who shifted the capital to Chamba and named it after his daughter Champavati. Chamba is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in HP. The Chamba rulers were great patrons of art, painting, and temple architecture. Famous Chamba Rumal (embroidery) and the Basholi/Chamba schools of painting owe their origin to royal patronage. Chamba remained a princely state until its merger with India in 1948.

The Mughals had significant influence over the Himalayan foothills although they could not effectively control the deeper hill regions due to difficult terrain. Key developments during the Mughal period include:

items: Emperor Akbar received tributes from several hill chiefs and had diplomatic relations with the Kangra raja.
The Kangra Fort was captured by Mughal general Shaikh Farid in 1620 CE under Emperor Jahangir.
Emperor Jahangir visited Kangra in 1622 CE and mentions the fort in his memoirs 'Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri'.
Shah Jahan faced revolts from hill chiefs.
After Aurangzeb's death (1707), Mughal control weakened rapidly; hill states reasserted independence.
The Sikh Gurus had strong connections with the HP region. Guru Gobind Singh spent time in the Naina Devi area and the Dhamdhar region.

blocks.content: The Gurkhas from Nepal invaded the hill states in the early 19th century. Under General Amar Singh Thapa, they occupied large parts of the western Himalayas including Kangra, Kullu, Mandi, and Sirmaur by 1806. Sikh forces under Dewan Mohkam Chand drove out the Gurkhas from Kangra in 1809. The Anglo-Gurkha War (1814–16) ended Gurkha expansion; the Treaty of Sugauli (1816) defined Nepal's western boundary.

After defeating the Gurkhas, the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh extended influence over the hills. Kangra Fort and several hill states paid tribute. After Ranjit Singh's death (1839) and the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46), the Treaty of Lahore (March 1846) transferred Jalandhar Doab and the hill territories south of the Beas to the British East India Company.

blocks.content: The freedom struggle in HP had a unique character combining resistance in British-administered districts and Praja Mandal movements in princely states.

items: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): Participated in British-administered Kangra and Shimla hills.
Mandi Conspiracy Case (1914): Bhai Hirda Ram and others plotted against British rule. Considered HP's most significant revolutionary act.
Praja Mandal Movements (1930s–1940s): Movements in Mandi, Bilaspur, Suket, Chamba, Sirmaur demanding democratic rights and responsible government.
Palampur Session of All India States' People Conference (1945): Boosted the movement.
Simon Commission (1928): Protests in HP's British areas.
Quit India Movement (1942): Active participation in Shimla hills region.
Key Leaders: Dr. Y.S. Parmar, Padam Dev (Mandi), Bhai Hirda Ram, Shiv Nand Ramaul (Shimla), Thakur Sen Negi (Kinnaur).
